papers.title: Mesenchymal stem cell-derived spheroids and microtissues for biofabrication: advances in bioassembly and bioprinting strategies.
papers.abstract: Biofabrication integrates biological and engineering principles to generate functional tissues for regenerative medicine, drug screening, and disease modeling. Among the diverse cellular sources available, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have emerged as a critical component due to their multipotency, immunomodulatory capacity, and scalability. This review focuses on MSC-derived spheroids and microtissues as building blocks for biofabrication, organizing recent advances in bioassembly and bioprinting strategies around the axis of undifferentiated versus pre-differentiated microtissues and how the timing of differentiation shapes construct functionality. Key technological innovations, including dynamic culture systems, scaffold-free assembly, and high-resolution bioprinting (e.g. droplet-based), have enabled enhanced control over microtissue maturation and structural fidelity. The role of the cellular microenvironment in determining MSC fate is examined, emphasizing how biochemical cues, mechanical properties, and oxygen gradients can be engineered during microtissue formation. Cellular heterogeneity is addressed as a path-dependent variable continuously reshaped by donor-specific factors (age, sex, health status) and process-imposed cues (isolation methods, expansion conditions, and mechanical stress) throughout thein vitrolife cycle, and concrete mitigation strategies are discussed, including prospective cell sorting and a proposed functional potency panel (extracellular matrix deposition, fusion competence, and secretome profiling), alongside recent advancements in automated and machine learning-based biofabrication platforms. Vascularization and immunological integration are examined as central translation bottlenecks, covering endothelial co-culture, prevascularized spheroids, sacrificial bioprinting, and MSC-driven modulation of the host immune response. By integrating the fabrication route, heterogeneity as a manufacturing process variable, and translational/regulatory bottlenecks into a single framework, this review highlights recent advances, discusses current limitations, and outlines future directions for clinical translation of MSC-based biofabrication.

papers.title: world2vec: Mechanistic world models through latent dynamics learning
papers.abstract: World models can achieve strong control performance without faithfully capturing the dynamics of their environment, limiting their potential for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery. Here, we introduce world2vec to learn mechanistic world models without reward information directly from observations and actions. World2vec learns latent dynamics that faithfully reproduce the true system over long prediction horizons, with at least one order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and LeWM. This enables state of the art performance in controlling continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors, demonstrating how world models are amenable to scientific discovery.

papers.title: Fight World Model: Customizable Combat through Visual Interaction Proxies
papers.abstract: A playable, programmable game world must maintain persistent state, enforce executable rules, and support extensible gameplay mechanics. Existing video world models can generate plausible combat, yet struggle to keep hit reactions and health updates consistent with game rules. We introduce Fight World Model (FWM), which separates rule-governed combat execution from video rendering. An executable engine maintains state and resolves interactions. A deterministic compiler encodes these outcomes and attempted actions in a spatially and temporally aligned interaction proxy. The proxy aligns action and skill windows, brief hit reactions, and persistent health by fighter identity and timing. These cues can be controlled separately to render interactions under modified rules. Identity-bound references preserve character appearance across side switches. We train FWM on FightWorld Corpus, spanning 52 skill effects, 187 character-appearance variants, and 15 arenas. Without retraining the renderer, FWM supports damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, lifesteal, and multi-stage skill mechanisms beyond the native game. It also allows character and arena customization. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FWM, which outperforms existing game world models in action fidelity, hit reactions, health-state consistency, and character appearance preservation. Our project is available at https://fight-world-model.github.io.

papers.title: NEOPIC: A Neural Operator Framework for Particle-based Kinetic Plasma Simulations
papers.abstract: We introduce NEOPIC, a framework for learning the field operator in particle-based methods applied to kinetic plasma simulations. Its key novelty is a neural operator that acts directly on the empirical measure of the particles, rather than on a grid, and is evaluated at the particle positions. No mesh or tree is needed and, unlike grid-based neural operators, no deposition onto a mesh takes place, so the particle noise that dominates the inputs of particle simulations is not aliased. Since it replaces only the field solve, it serves as a plug-and-play field solver for particle-based methods: it can be trained on data from particle-in-cell, particle-in-Fourier or tree codes, and combined with any time integrator, including implicit schemes. We prove that the discrete evaluation coincides with the continuous operator at any number of particles (representation equivalence) and derive an error analysis that separates sampling, learning and time-stepping errors: up to the learning error, NEOPIC has the error structure of standard Monte Carlo particle methods. We show that the particle noise in the training data acts as an implicit regularizer, which gives guidance on the number of training particles in relation to the particle numbers used at inference. A complexity analysis shows that NEOPIC is an $O(N_p)$ method whose constants are set by the architecture alone, independently of any mesh or tree. Numerical experiments on electrostatic benchmarks in two and three dimensions, including Landau damping, two-stream and bump-on-tail instabilities, a cyclotron mini-app and a Penning trap, confirm the theoretical findings. A single model trained on several mini-apps generated by different reference methods captures all of them and remains stable up to twice the training time window, which points towards foundation models for fields in particle-based methods.

papers.title: Algebraic World Model: From Exploration to Proofs
papers.abstract: AI has made remarkable progress in mathematics, solving challenging problems with machine-checkable proofs in Lean, yet typically relying on predefined mathematical definitions and formal specifications. This raises a natural question: can it reason rigorously about an unknown world? We introduce the Algebraic World Model (AWM), a framework that turns interaction with unfamiliar environments into explicit mathematical models supporting formal reasoning. AWM explores the environment and develops executable Python hypotheses, continually testing and revising them against observations. It then structures these hypotheses into typed objects and shared rules, simplifies their structure through category-theory-guided transformations, and formalizes the resulting model in Lean 4 to prove reachability and impossibility. AWM can formally prove that a goal is unreachable, even beyond explored trajectories. On two impossible game levels, it constructs closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs excluding every legal winning sequence in all six runs, while Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, equipped with coding tools, produce none in twelve baseline runs. Four of AWM's six initial bounds are correct, compared with one for Opus 5.5 and none for GPT-6 Astra; given only feedback that a cheaper win exists, AWM revises its rules and constructs new proofs, reaching six of six correct bounds. Moreover, AWM produces interpretable mathematical models whose rules can be inspected and tested step by step. Across all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, these models enable Lean to replay the winning trajectories of all 183 levels and generalize beyond observed play, predicting unseen transitions and detecting changes in game mechanics. With Claude Opus 5, AWM clears all levels with a score of 99.9, while its certified winning trajectories use only 43% of the human baseline's actions.

papers.title: Accurate MRI-free PET Quantification and Reliability Assessment via CT-to-MRI Synthesis and Conformal Prediction
papers.abstract: Standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR) quantification of amyloid PET commonly relies on a subject-specific T1-weighted MRI, yet a usable MRI is not always available. We therefore combined CT-to-MRI synthesis with conformal prediction for MRI-free PET quantification with reliability assessment. A slice-consistent Brownian Bridge Diffusion Model was strengthened with multi-dataset training and data-source conditioning to enrich the anatomical prior learned from MRI, and with expanded multi-slice CT context to exploit the through-plane continuity of subject-specific anatomy in CT. Synthetic MRI was used for FreeSurfer-based anatomical parcellation and PET quantification, while deep-ensemble uncertainty was calibrated with conformal prediction to estimate a plausible range for the corresponding real MRI-based SUVR. On $^{11}$C-PiB PET from OASIS-3, the proposed method achieved the highest synthesis and parcellation fidelity among the compared methods. Mean cortical SUVR from the proposed synthetic MRI agreed closely with the real MRI-based reference (MAE $0.016 \pm 0.015$, Pearson $r = 0.9987$) and yielded the same amyloid-positivity classification as the real MRI in all 87 test subjects at the prespecified cut-off. Conformal prediction achieved empirical coverage close to the prespecified levels, and at 90% target coverage, 85 of 87 subjects had prediction intervals that supported an unambiguous amyloid-positivity decision. Zero-shot evaluation on an independent external cohort showed that the proposed CT-to-MRI model could support PET quantification without retraining, although conformal calibration required target-cohort recalibration to recover the intended coverage. These findings support CT-to-MRI-based MRI-free PET quantification as a promising approach for providing accurate SUVR measurements and an explicit assessment of their reliability.

papers.title: Training language models in simulation for psychiatric intake
papers.abstract: In psychiatric practice, the clinical intake interview remains a primary diagnostic instrument, requiring the clinician to establish rapport while disentangling complex, overlapping presentations. Here, we show that multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation environments improves language model performance on structured text-based psychiatric intake, spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning. In a randomized, double-blind crossover study ($N = 60$ matched scenario pairs, 120 encounters) comparing the RL-trained agent against its identically prompted base model, 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients while a separate panel of 15 independent, board-certified psychiatrists scored the de-identified transcripts. The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs ($p < 0.0001$), with gains on an adapted clinical-examination rubric ($d_z = 0.77$, $p < 0.0001$), patient-centered communication (82.0% vs. 65.2%, $p < 0.001$), and differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3%, $p < 0.001$). Across 127 psychiatrist-validated simulated intake scenarios, the trained agent nearly doubled its base model's clinical rubric score (0.706 vs. 0.379; composite reward 0.564 vs. 0.294, $p < 0.0001$). To systematically probe conversational safety, we established two Delphi-consensus taxonomies, of clinical safety risks and relational competencies, from which 256 challenging adversarial presentations were derived; we find that training in simulation environments more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks (12.9% vs. 30.5%, $p < 0.0001$). Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters, though residual gaps require safeguards and clinician oversight.

papers.title: Reinforcement learning for control of partial differential equations
papers.abstract: Controlling dynamical systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs) remains a challenging task in scientific computing, owing to high-dimensional state spaces, distributed actuation, nonlinear dynamics, and stringent real-time constraints. Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for synthesizing feedback controllers that adapt to varying operating conditions and can be deployed efficiently in real-time. This review provides a unified perspective on RL and PDE-constrained optimization, and surveys model-free, model-based, and multi-agent RL approaches to PDE control, with particular emphasis on sample efficiency, generalization across parametric variations, and scalability to high-dimensional problems. Two demonstrative examples, the stabilization of a chaotic system and a flow control problem, illustrate the performance and pitfalls of RL agents in practice. Finally, we discuss evaluation and benchmarking practices, current limitations, and open research directions toward reliable, data-efficient, and scalable RL for scientific computing.

papers.title: Uncertainty-aware Feedback Loop Diagnosis: integrating reinforcement learning and conformal prediction for reliable wafer defect classification
papers.abstract: Semiconductor manufacturing is a complex, multi-step process that requires both high precision and low operating costs. Therefore, detecting defects in a high-volume setting is an important component of wafer map analysis for reliable production. However, most state-of-the-art deep learning approaches require a full scan of the surface, which hinders the development of high-throughput inspection systems. To address this problem, we propose Uncertainty-aware Feedback Loop Diagnosis (UFLD), a novel algorithm that employs reinforcement learning for adaptive measurement acquisition and provides a prediction uncertainty level after each step, stopping the process once sufficient information is obtained. Unlike existing methods that rely on ensemble models or auxiliary confidence estimation deep learning models, UFLD utilizes a more parameter-efficient conformal prediction framework to determine the optimal stopping time. The proposed UFLD reduces acquisition time by about $40\%$ and achieves $98.4\%$ inspection accuracy, without requiring an additional learned confidence-estimation network. We validated our approach on the MixedWM38 dataset, demonstrating its advantages over existing adaptive acquisition procedures and standard convolutional neural networks.

papers.title: The Athlete as a Scientist of One: Agentic Bayesian Experimental Design for Individualized Physiology from Consumer Wearables
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for personal health read wearable data and recommend, but do not learn about the individual in a way that can be audited or falsified. We present EpiCoach, an agentic system that treats one athlete, a cross-country mountain biker, as the subject of accountable N-of-1 science. Claims about the athlete live in an evidence-gated hypothesis registry: each must issue a probabilistic prediction about a future session before it occurs, and its belief moves only through computed evidence from a logged statistical fit. Predictions come from a mechanistic digital twin inferred from heart rate, GPS and barometric altitude: a lagged heart-rate response model, a fitness-fatigue model with learned time constants, and a latent technical-descending skill state, measured on discovered trail segments. The agent prescribes the next training week as a constrained experiment maximizing information gain subject to load and safety constraints, around two instrument rides. We evaluate the system two ways over eighteen months of data. A rolling-origin replay benchmark shows the twin beats standard forecasters on heart rate but not segment time, and the agentic loop matches a static model. A live prospective phase runs the weekly cycle: in its first three weeks the ledger sealed 20 predictions, scored 14, the descent forecast calibrated after one correction, the climb forecast pessimistic as the athlete improved, and the safety officer vetoed the agent twice. Every correction is preserved in the registry, a template for auditable, falsifiable personalization in digital health. We release the registry, benchmark and protocol.

papers.title: Wizard: Manipulate Any World in Real Time via Agentic Control
papers.abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled the generation of increasingly realistic and interactive virtual environments, opening new possibilities for player-customizable gameplay. Agentic frameworks further advance this direction by decoupling explicit game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. However, existing approaches support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters, and offer limited real-time interactivity. In this paper, we introduce Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, precise control over character motions while generalizing zero-shot across novel scenes, characters, and actions. To achieve this, we construct a diverse dataset spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters, incorporating skeleton and geometry information as structured representations. We leverage these representations as intermediate proxies to condition a video generation model, together with an adaptive masking mechanism that improves alignment between the conditioning signals and generated video rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce an agentic framework that explicitly maintains and updates game states, allowing players to freely configure their virtual worlds and exercise fine-grained control over character motions while preserving visual quality and gameplay consistency. By combining agentic control with structured proxy-based generation, our framework unlocks new possibilities for player-driven game creation with real-time, generalizable, and mechanically consistent world simulation.

papers.title: Neighborhood Elites: Quality-Diversity Search for Uncertainty Quantification in Question Answering
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, yet they produce wrong answers indistinguishable from correct ones. In question answering (QA), such an error propagates unnoticed into downstream tasks. Perturbation-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) addresses this by probing a model over a set of input rewrites and reading uncertainty from how much its predictions vary. Yet this set is usually built generically, by free paraphrasing, token-level perturbation, or adversarial search. Such rewrites leave two things uncontrolled that matter in QA: what kind of change is made to the context, and how explicitly the context supports the answer. When neither is controlled, the composition of the set is determined by the generator rather than by design, and the estimate inherits whatever that generator happens to produce. Quality-diversity (QD) search is built to cover a predefined exploration space, so we recast input perturbation as a QD problem and propose \emph{neighborhood elites (NE)}, a neighborhood constructor that spreads answer-preserving rewrites across two axes, the kind of edit and the explicitness of support. We compare NE against three other neighborhood constructors, holding the editor, QA model, uncertainty measure and search objective fixed, and against three scores read from the original context. Across five extractive-QA datasets and five instruction-tuned LLMs, NE improves failure detection against every other constructor in at least 24 of the 25 dataset-model pairs, reaching 0.726 AUROC and 0.211 AUPRC lift over the base rate. Additionally, NE detects failure better than semantic entropy computed over decoder samples, by 0.074 AUROC and 0.062 AUPRC lift, and this advantage widens as the neighborhood grows.

papers.abstract: Autonomous highway driving for heavy-duty trucks is a challenging control problem. The greater mass, dimensions and intricate dynamics increase the requirements for cooperation from surrounding traffic in critical maneuvers, requiring a careful balance between safety constraints and efficient long-horizon decision making. Model Predictive Control (MPC) provides rigorous constraint satisfaction but relies on terminal cost which can limit its effectiveness at short, computationally affordable horizons. Reinforcement Learning (RL) captures long-term driving behavior but offers no constraint guarantees and tends toward overly conservative policies when trained under sparse collision penalties. In this paper, we propose a hybrid MPC and RL framework for highway driving in autonomous trucks, where a finite-horizon MPC, solved via dynamic programming, uses a pre-trained RL model for terminal cost estimation. We evaluate the framework in a simulation environment with reactive surrounding traffic and compare it against pure MPC with zero terminal cost, rollout with terminal cost estimation using a base policy, and pure RL. Results show that the hybrid approach achieves zero collisions with the lowest cost of any configuration.

papers.title: A Deep Learning Framework for Quantile Demand Forecasting in E-commerce with Doubly Censored Data

Moreover, quantile estimation has gained widespread application as it offers valuable uncertainty quantification, thereby enhancing the robustness of decision-making processes. However, limited research has addressed the effective quantification of uncertainty when target labels are ambiguous. In retail, actual sales can be capped by stock and boosted by temporary promotions, whereas the target is underlying demand. Such scenarios are characterized by double censoring and no deep-learning pipeline yet exists for such data. In this paper, we introduce a straightforward framework for learning quantiles from doubly-censored observations and propose a tailored evaluation metric. Our approach is supported by theoretical guarantees, and we empirically demonstrate that our metric correlates well with the oracle calibration measure. Experimental results show that our estimator surpasses existing baselines. Finally, inventory simulations and real-world applications confirm the practical utility of our method in retail operations.

papers.title: Does System Size Matter in Uncertainty Quantification for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials?
papers.abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) commonly use uncertainty estimates to flag out-of-distribution (OOD) configurations and select structures for active learning. A key question is whether the resulting structure-level uncertainty scores remain comparable across different system sizes. A common practice is to aggregate per-atom uncertainties by their mean or maximum and compare the resulting score against a fixed threshold, implicitly assuming such comparability. We test this assumption across several in-distribution (ID)/OOD pairs by characterizing both aggregations as a function of atom count. The two aggregations exhibit distinct size dependencies. Mean aggregation remains size-independent for homogeneous systems but loses sensitivity to defects in large cells. In contrast, maximum aggregation grows with system size for ID systems while remaining approximately flat for defect-containing systems, narrowing the ID-OOD gap in a manner consistent with extreme-value statistics. Although highly uncertain atoms in large structures may indicate novel local environments, retraining on these structures yields little improvement, in contrast to retraining on OOD structures constructed to lie outside the training distribution. Our results reveal a practical limitation of size-unaware uncertainty criteria and motivate size-aware calibration for more reliable OOD detection in large-scale atomistic simulations.

papers.title: Humanoid Dodgeball: Learning Fast Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance Motions for Humanoids
papers.abstract: Humanoids have become increasingly agile and capable in real-world environments. Our method enables highly dynamic whole-body evasive maneuvers against incoming projectiles through threat-aware reward shaping, while multiple direction-specific adversarial motion priors regularize the learned behaviors toward stable and diverse human-like motions. Extensive simulation and hardware experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework substantially improves dynamic obstacle avoidance performance across diverse obstacle speeds and launch distances, while preserving robust and physically plausible humanoid motions.

papers.title: Probabilistic Meshless Methods on Manifolds
papers.abstract: Probabilistic meshless methods solve partial differential equations (PDEs) by placing a Gaussian process prior on the solution and conditioning it on the PDE at a finite set of collocation nodes. The posterior provides both an approximation of the solution and a Bayesian quantification of its error. While these methods are well established on Euclidean domains, their extension to manifolds lacks, to our knowledge, any convergence analysis. We extend them to compact manifolds and study their convergence in two settings. First, for known manifolds whose Laplace-Beltrami eigenpairs are available, the prior can be evaluated exactly, but the PDE operator generally cannot be applied to it in closed form. We replace this operator by a standard generalized finite difference discretization on a point cloud sampled from the manifold, and show that the resulting method is consistent at the points of the cloud, at a rate governed by their fill distance. Second, for implicit manifolds, known only through a point cloud, both the prior and the operator must be approximated. We propose a new generalized finite difference scheme with a free stencil radius, and show that it retains the consistency of the standard construction while controlling the growth of its coefficients, and that an appropriate radius yields uniform convergence of the discrete Gram matrix. In both settings, we derive error bounds for the posterior mean which separate the collocation error intrinsic to the method from the error due to approximating the operator and, for implicit manifolds, the prior. Experiments on the circle, the sphere and the flat torus confirm our theoretical claims. On real-world cortical thickness data, our approach attains the accuracy of established discretizations, while conditioning on fewer than a tenth of the observations and providing a credible interval at every vertex.

papers.title: A Semigroup-Aware Kernel Neural Operator with Latent Exponential Integration for Forced PDEs
papers.abstract: We propose a semigroup-aware structured kernel neural operator for source-driven evolution PDEs. Unlike generic time-conditioned kernel models, the proposed formulation represents temporal dependence through a latent exponential propagator \(e^{tA_θ}\), where \(A_θ\) is a learned latent generator. This provides a structured transition from a non-ODE kernel representation to an ODE-inspired kernel operator whose latent temporal evolution satisfies the composition principle of evolution semigroups. For time-dependent forcing terms, a direct kernel-based evaluation requires repeated quadrature over delayed kernel evaluations. To address this computational bottleneck, we derive a latent-first reformulation of the source term: the forcing field is projected onto the kernel-induced latent space, where its accumulated effect is represented as the solution of a forced linear latent dynamical system. For a fixed learned kernel, this reformulation is exact. The resulting system can then be integrated using a \(φ_1\)-based exponential integrator, yielding a source-evaluation path that is structurally aligned with the learned latent propagator. The resulting framework combines geometry- and physics-conditioned low-rank kernel factorization with alternative source-evaluation paths based on either explicit Duhamel quadrature or latent exponential integration. Dissipativity constraints on the latent generator and identity-preserving corrections near the initial time are optional architectural components. Numerical experiments on advection-iffusion-reaction (ADR) problems compare the non-ODE and semigroup-aware formulations, evaluate the quadrature and \(φ_1\) source paths, and assess predictive accuracy and computational cost.

To this end, we introduce a possibility-based contrastive grade of prediction as an alternative quantification method to existing latent posterior-based approaches for parameter estimation (approximation) and model selection. Unlike conventional Bayesian inference, which represents uncertainty within the probabilistic framework, the proposed model adopts a possibility-based representation that allows uncertain and potentially conflicting information to be characterized more flexibly. Rather than focusing on isolated aspects of a problem, the resulting mathematical framework provides a systematic approach to data mining while mitigating overly confident, yet implausible predictions generated by highly specialized deep learning architectures.

papers.title: Surrogate Uncertainty for Black-box Visual Grounding
papers.abstract: Visual grounding is crucial for robots to understand language instructions with visual observations. This paper addresses the problem of visual grounding uncertainties, where a robot uses a black-box vision-language model (VLM) to ground free-form natural-language instructions to target objects. Prevailing methods derive uncertainty from the VLM itself. Yet, outputs of the VLM, e.g., generated uncertainties, are from the same parameters and structures producing the predictions, and inherit the bias. We give a formal Bayesian definition of the problem that treats the VLM prediction as an observation. An external surrogate Bayesian model then quantifies per-query uncertainty over a local neighborhood of a held-out calibration set, decomposed into aleatoric and epistemic components. A hierarchical retrieval across input modalities realizes a compact joint-space neighborhood, mitigating the curse of dimensionality. papers.title: Data-Driven or Model-Constrained? Comparing Airflow Estimation Methods under Sparse Sensing
papers.abstract: Airflow-driven advection is the primary mechanism for gas and aerosol dispersion in real-world scenarios, making accurate airflow estimation essential for ventilation monitoring, gas source localization, and contaminant spread analysis. Since obtaining airflow maps via high-resolution spatial sensing is usually infeasible in practice, flow field estimation methods must cope with sparse measurements by introducing statistical or physical priors to compensate for limited data. Existing approaches mainly differ in how they incorporate fluid-flow constraints and environmental geometry. However, due to the lack of systematic comparisons across this spectrum of methods, the potential benefits of physics-based priors for airflow estimation under sparse sensing remain underexplored. To address this question, we quantitatively evaluate four airflow estimators across three simulated 2D scenarios under steady-state conditions and varying sampling densities. The methods range from Gaussian Process Regression and graph-based Gaussian Markov Random Fields to two Navier-Stokes-based approaches, including a novel strong-form residual minimization variant. Our results show that physical priors provide the greatest benefit at low sampling densities by compensating for missing spatial information. Although data-driven Gaussian Process Regression becomes increasingly competitive as sensor coverage increases, model-based estimators retain an accuracy advantage across the evaluated scenarios.

papers.abstract: We propose a modern all-at-once framework for PDE-based Bayesian inversion by introducing the PDE residual as probabilistic information. Theoretically, we establish the well-posedness of the posterior with uncertainty quantification, and numerically, we propose two efficiency inversion algorithms based on two posterior sampling methods. In particular, one algorithm is based on Metropolis-within-Gibbs MCMC method with a PDE-informed block- diagonal Gaussian prior, and the other is based on a joint sampling strategy. Numerical experiments for a semiconductor inverse problem confirm that the proposed Bayesian all-at-once approach yields a speedup of approximately a factor of two, while having a comparable reconstruction quality as the conventional reduced-based setting.

papers.title: Learning Kolmogorov Backward Operators for Spectral Analysis and Forecasting: A Data-Driven Variational Galerkin Framework
papers.abstract: For a time-homogeneous Markov process, the fixed-lag solution operator \( (T_τf)(x)=\mathbb E[f(X_{t+τ})\mid X_t=x] \) of the Kolmogorov backward equation evolves observables linearly and deterministically, even when the dynamics are stochastic. We approximate this operator using a two-stage method where we first approximate this operator directly from data, without knowledge of the governing equation (e.g., Fourier Neural Operator), and then compress the Galerkin projection onto a finite-dimensional observable space that is fixed in advance or selected variationally. The error analysis traces the learning error of the estimator, the sampling error of the Galerkin inner products, and the invariance and reconstruction properties of the observable space to the computed spectra and forecasts. The sampling error enters only through a multiplicative factor. Near an isolated spectral cluster, the invariance defect of a subspace controls its distance from the target invariant subspace. The forecast error is controlled by the one-step error of the reduced model and the projection error of the observable; when the measure is invariant and the reduced model preserves constants and is stable on mean-zero observables, the bound is uniform in the horizon. For deterministic dynamics, a learning rate for Fourier neural operators (FNOs) gives one explicit bound for the learning error. Numerical experiments illustrate spectral approximation and forecasting, including long-rollout stability and a comparison with extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD) when fewer transition pairs than basis functions are observed.

papers.title: TabCUQ: Context-Uncertainty Quantification for Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models use in-context learning to estimate conditional expected outcomes and average treatment effects for specific groups of individuals. Using these estimates to guide scientific decisions requires reliable uncertainty quantification. The challenge is to account simultaneously for two sources of uncertainty: limited-context bias and context variation arising from the small labeled sample supplied at inference. Predictive spread does not directly quantify both sources of uncertainty, and we observe that the ordinary bootstrap may substantially overestimate context variation, whereas subsampling may underestimate it. We introduce TabCUQ, a perturbation-based framework that injects noise into observed outcomes and applies the foundation model to the perturbed contexts. TabCUQ estimates context variation using wild-bootstrap dispersion and accounts for limited-context bias using the maximum deviation between perturbed and original estimates. For a kernel-regression analogue whose estimation error admits an exact decomposition into these two components, we show that our framework provides asymptotically valid pointwise coverage. In simulations, TabCUQ substantially improves coverage, with average interval widths typically about twice those of an oracle bias-aware benchmark. Across seven real-world tasks, it also improves coverage of reference functions learned from much larger samples.

papers.title: Non-Asymptotic Confidence Regions for Separable Nonlinear Models
papers.abstract: This paper studies robust uncertainty quantification for separable nonlinear least squares (SNLLS) problems. We propose two identification methods, (i) Residual-Perturbed Gradient (RPG) and (ii) Global-Fit-Gap (GFG), to construct joint distribution-free confidence regions for both the linear and nonlinear parameters. By exploiting assumed group invariance of the noise (such as symmetry or exchangeability), we apply random perturbations (such as sign-changes or permutations) to build the regions based on resampling and ranking. We prove that both methods guarantee non-asymptotically exact coverage (type I error). Finally, we illustrate the constructions through two numerical experiments: (i) identifying generalized finite impulse response (GFIR) systems using Laguerre polynomials with an adjustable decay rate and (ii) fitting Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) models with variable knots and widths.

papers.title: Robust LIDAR Sensor-to-Sensor Domain Generalization via Accumulated-Point Scene Completion
papers.abstract: We study domain generalization for LIDAR semantic segmentation. Deep neural networks achieve strong performance on 3D point clouds, yet real-world LIDAR exhibits sensor-specific sampling patterns that hinder transfer across datasets. In many applications, performance on completely unseen sensors is crucial. A model should preferably work on a new setup without prior access to its data or labels. To this end, we introduce a source-only training scheme that adds an occupancy prediction auxiliary objective. We aggregate source-domain scans into a simple world model and use it as the supervision signal, replacing single-scan standard segmentation training.   A key property of our approach is that it does not alter the input scan. During training and testing the network consumes the same single-frame LIDAR input, only the supervision signal is enriched via the occupancy objective. At deployment, there is no runtime overhead as the auxiliary head can be dropped for pure segmentation, or kept to obtain scene completion alongside semantic segmentation. In an experimental evaluation across distinct LIDAR datasets, we demonstrate that a model's generalization to new domains can be significantly affected by how it is supervised. In certain setups, performance on unseen domains improves without any explicit domain adaptation (no target scans, no target labels, no sensor priors) and without prediction refinement. At the same time, our method maintains competitive source-domain segmentation performance and incurs no additional inference cost.

papers.title: WorldFlow: Joint Video and 3D Motion Prediction via Large-Scale Pretraining
papers.abstract: Predicting future physical states stands as a central challenge in embodied intelligence. Existing video world models leave 3D dynamics implicit, action-based formulations remain tied to specific robot configurations, and 3D motion prediction models use flow-only supervision, providing a limited learning signal for physical dynamics. To circumvent these limitations, we introduce \method{}, a generative world model that jointly predicts future video and query-based 3D trajectories. By parameterizing 3D motion as continuous displacement tokens aligned with the video grid, a unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone jointly denoises both modalities under a rectified-flow objective. This formulation couples explicit geometric dynamics with visual evolution, effectively unlocking the physical commonsense embedded within pretrained video models. To empirically scale and validate this unified architecture, we train \method{} on a heterogeneous mixture of 1.44 million object-level samples spanning simulated and real-world domains. We further introduce WorldFlowBench, comprising 1,678 evaluation samples from 11 data sources across simulated and real-world interactions, including spatial reasoning tasks. Across all three evaluation sets, WorldFlow achieves the lowest average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) among the evaluated learning-based methods. Notably, on the challenging SpatialCog set, WorldFlow achieves an ADE of 0.060 m, a 54.2\% reduction compared with the strongest external baseline. It also reduces ADE and FDE by 55.9\% and 68.5\%, respectively, compared with its flow-only variant. Project page: https://worldflow-rbs.github.io/.

papers.title: LLM-Assisted Optimization for Simulation-Based Redesign
papers.abstract: Engineering design frequently involves redesigning a prior solution to adapt to changes in context, such as material prices or system requirements. Redesign often leverages simulators too complex and/or computationally intensive for traditional numerical solvers, which lack engineering knowledge and context, to ensure global solution quality. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret semantic information, including engineering knowledge about the system and changes in context, to help guide search, and recent studies have shown that incorporating this knowledge into optimization can improve search performance. However, how best to combine LLMs with numerical solvers in redesign remains unclear. We develop and test an integrated LLM-optimization approach for redesign and compare three methods for leveraging LLMs (warm start, variable fixing and ReAct) and four black-box solvers (Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, mesh adaptive direct search and random search) on an electric vehicle battery pack cost minimization case study across four types of redesign scenarios. We find that the integrated approach can match feasible design discovery of the numerical-solver baselines with 80% fewer simulator evaluations while tripling the fraction of runs that find near-optimal solutions. We find that the best LLM-solver integration approach and the way the prior solution is leveraged depend on the structure of the design requirement change, and that the benefit of increasing LLM model size grows with the extent to which the LLM controls the search. These results show clear potential for LLMs in redesign tasks for guiding or replacing numerical solvers.

GenSight uses a unified spatiotemporal representation for video, depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow. Built on a shared DiT backbone, GenSight uses lightweight task modulation to predict all modalities within the same architecture. All tasks are jointly optimized within a unified velocity prediction space. At inference, GenSight supports two complementary modes: multi-step future video generation with aligned dense predictions and single-step dense perception from an observed video. By unifying modality representation, model architecture, and prediction space, GenSight avoids separate modality-specific pipelines and couples appearance, geometry, semantics, and motion in a shared representation. It promotes cross-modal consistency and allows dense perception to benefit from the spatiotemporal priors learned through video generation. Trained on embodied manipulation data spanning multiple robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, GenSight demonstrates strong performance in both video generation and dense 4D perception, highlighting the effectiveness of unifying seeing and imagining for embodied world modeling.

papers.abstract: Learning from offline datasets is limited in scalability, as collecting new experience is often costly or unsafe in the real world. To this end, we propose using the world model as a local transition generator, leveraging critic guidance to choose actions inside that model to generate synthetic experiences. We study action refinement methodologies, introducing Critic-Guided Synthetic Experience (CGSE) generation in world models. Specifically, CGSE augments an existing offline dataset by sampling candidate actions using an offline policy and refining each to maximize a first-order approximation of the $Q$-function within a trust region. We then use a frozen latent world model to imagine the future state given each updated action, and use the critic to choose the best one, appending this synthetic transition to the replay buffer. Our method requires no additional real-environment interaction or test-time planner, as it generates synthetic experience offline using the world model. On three OGBench manipulation tasks, CGSE improves an offline policy by a relative improvement of $7.1\%$ on the average success rate.

papers.title: Tactus: Tactile & Pose Sensing Glove for Natural Dexterity Data Collection
papers.abstract: Collecting naturalistic human manipulation demonstrations with accurate contact force and hand pose is essential for robot dexterous manipulation policy and foundational world model learning - yet no existing wearable platform provides both calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a form factor that preserves natural manipulation behavior. We present Tactus, a textile-integrated sensing glove that co-optimizes three design pillars: (1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5 mm fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation, (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies, and (3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable. Tactus includes a documented calibration pipeline for cross-glove consistency and per-session calibration for subject-dependent correction. To enable objective comparison, we introduce standardized benchmarking protocols for tactile force regression and hand pose estimation, and apply them to Tactus and two commercially available tactile gloves - to our knowledge the first quantitative cross-platform evaluation of this kind. Tactus resolves a minimum detectable force of 0.59 N at 95% confidence, 1.6 - 2.7x lower than the commercial baselines, and with 0.87 cross-participant consistency, while our pose tracking sustains 11.0 mm fingertip keypoint relative error during manipulation, when occlusion is heaviest. We show that these combined signals support object property estimation, slip detection, and representative recording of hand-object interaction - yielding demonstration data with the fidelity required for contact-aware manipulation policies and world models.

papers.title: Certified Access: Test-Time Compute on Conservative Physics-Structured AI Memory
papers.abstract: Test-time compute mechanisms, such as retries, confidence-based escalation and non-local routing, are conventionally deployed as black-box additions to trained models. They typically add forward passes or halting heads, but give no structural account of what the extra compute buys or what it costs against the model's stability guarantees. We therefore propose a theoretical and empirical framework for test-time compute on a Latent Dynamics Model used as the memory. When an encoder's latent state $(q,p)$ is advanced by a damped symplectic (velocity-Verlet) step of a learned Hamiltonian, every mechanism that expands access has an exact phase-volume Jacobian, a bounded energy change and an exact latch-transport law. We split reachability failures into escape failures and reach failures. A Lorentz squeeze resolves escape failures by injecting bounded, re-absorbable energy. A gated canonical translation (a one-step channel across $C_T$) resolves reach failures at $\detJ=1$ exactly. We verify this certificate stack on a designed analytic testbed. Reaching just beyond $C_T$ with the squeeze requires energy that grows quadratically in the excess distance. The gated channel's energy cost equals the potential difference between its endpoints, which is zero on the matched channel measured here, and so does not grow with distance in this testbed. An untrained state-replacing map annihilates phase volume and erases stored charge, while the gated channel transports it. On a learned physics-structured memory, we show calibrated compute rationing and evaluate the scaling limits of non-local routing against a physics-free baseline. The main contribution is the formalization and verification of the certificate stack, not benchmark performance.

papers.title: Surface Roughness as a Determinant of the Immunological Tissue Response to Additively Manufactured Titanium Implants
papers.abstract: Background/Aim: Surface roughness strongly affects host responses to titanium implants. Additive manufacturing (AM) by selective laser melting (SLM) allows controlled surface generation but the immune consequences of AM-derived roughness remain unclear. Materials and Methods: Three AM titanium disks with distinct roughness were analyzed by scanning electron microscopy and profilometry. At 10 and 30 days after subcutaneous implantation of disks in rats, tissue responses were evaluated according to ISO 10993-6. A novel phagocyte accumulation index (PAI) was applied, integrating mononuclear infiltration, multinucleated giant cells, coverage, and morphology. Results: All specimens induced only mild to moderate inflammation, confirming biocompatibility. Histology showed fibrosis, macrophage persistence, and rare multinucleated giant cells, without intergroup differences by ISO scoring. In contrast, the PAI detected significant differences: high-roughness specimens showed the highest values at day 30, significantly exceeding those of medium-roughness surfaces (p<0.05), while low-roughness surfaces were intermediate in value. Conclusion: The PAI revealed surface roughness-dependent differences in phagocytic activity not captured by ISO scoring. High-roughness AM surfaces promoted the strongest response, highlighting AM and its process parameters as a biological determinant and PAI as a sensitive tool for biomaterial evaluation.

papers.title: Implant Choice Impacts Initial Tibial Component Micromotion in Total Ankle Replacement
papers.abstract: Background: Total ankle replacements (TARs) have a risk of early mechanical failure. Clinical studies have shown that implants with more robust tibial fixation—i.e., stemmed designs—have a lower early mechanical failure risk. We aimed to compare the micromotion between 2 tibial components with different fixation features, using a cadaveric robotic gait simulator. We hypothesized that more robust fixation accommodates loads more effectively, resulting in less micromotion at the bone-implant interface for stemmed tibial implants when compared to low-profile tibial implants. Methods: Specimens from 10 cadaveric matched pairs (from 6 men and 4 women, age: 48 ± 11 years) were implanted with either a low-profile or stemmed TAR. Post-TAR, gait was simulated using a validated 6-degrees-of-freedom robot. A digital image correlation camera system captured the relative motion between the tibial bone and the implant via surface markers. Implant micromotion was calculated by performing rigid-body transformations on segmented geometries of the tibia and implant derived from computed tomography imaging. Peak and mean micromotion were defined as the maximum and mean nodal displacement, respectively, on the implant surface across all time points in stance. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests compared micromotion of stemmed and low-profile implants between matched pairs. Results: On average, peak and mean micromotion values were greater for low-profile implants by 150 µm (95% confidence interval [CI]: 98 to 203 µm) and 30 µm (95% CI: 9 to 52 µm), respectively, compared with the matched stemmed implants (p < 0.001 for both). Peak micromotion of low-profile implants typically occurred at the posterior aspect of the implant. In contrast, stemmed implants demonstrated a more evenly distributed pattern with peak micromotion located at the tip of the stem. Conclusions: This study identified significantly greater time-zero micromotion of low-profile tibial implants compared with stemmed implants. The micromotion distribution suggests that the stemmed implants were further compressed into bone, whereas the low-profile implants demonstrated a rocking motion. Our data support the notion that early mechanical failures of low-profile tibial implants may be due to excessive early micromotion. Level of Evidence: Therapeutic Level IV . See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

papers.title: 3D-printable and cytocompatible hydrogel from Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 extracellular matrix
papers.abstract: Abstract Tissue engineering has advanced significantly, yet multicomponent hydrogels inspired by the compositional complexity of natural extracellular matrices (ECMs) are still underexplored. Most current hydrogels are based on single-component formulations, which can limit their biochemical and mechanical versatility. Developing synthetic multicomponent hydrogels remains challenging because it requires the controlled integration of multiple functional groups within a single material platform. Here, a biologically driven strategy is introduced by leveraging Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1, a bacterium that naturally produces extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) composed of a multicomponent matrix of polysaccharides and proteins. Through three-day cultivation and a simple extraction method, a hydrogel is obtained that can be methacrylated and photocrosslinked using red or blue light. This hydrogel is porous, cytocompatible, 3D-bioprintable, injectable, and undergoes rapid gelation for in situ crosslinking. This work highlights the potential of using bacterial-derived multicomponent hydrogels for biofabrication.

Design/methodology/approach A new dimensionless number, Π, combines absorbed laser energy, track and layer overlap and heat-transfer effects. The framework is evaluated using experimental data from several alloys. Findings The relative-density data follow a common relative density (RD)–Π trend and reveal clear densification regions, including lack of fusion, rapid densification, near-full density and excessive energy input. Machine learning results confirm that Π alone captures the dominant mechanisms governing densification. Originality/value The proposed framework provides a simple, physically meaningful and transferable tool for LPBF process design. It offers an alternative to conventional energy-density measures and purely data-driven models.

papers.title: Optimisation of Metal Augments in Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty: Current Advances and Future Directions.
papers.abstract: Revision total hip arthroplasty (THA) is a challenging procedure, especially when addressing acetabular bone defects that compromise implant stability and long-term fixation. Metal augmentation is a common solution to restore structural integrity and ease implant placement. Recent literature has increasingly addressed clinical outcomes, porous implant technologies, and patient-specific reconstruction; however, an integrated perspective linking defect morphology, implant design, biomechanics, computational optimisation, manufacturing, and clinical translation remains limited. This narrative review critically discusses current metal augmentation technologies in terms of biomechanical performance, defect characteristics, and clinical outcomes. The main limitations, such as poor geometrical conformity, stress shielding, micromotion, and fixation failure, are discussed along with the role of computational modelling in evaluating implant behaviour. Critically, the review highlights the lack of integrated frameworks linking defect morphology, biomechanical performance, and clinical outcomes. Emerging technologies like additive manufacturing, patient-specific implants, and digital modelling are discussed from a translational perspective. It also emphasises the need for clinically validated, biomechanics-driven evaluation strategies to guide acetabular reconstruction and improve patient outcomes in revision THA.

papers.title: Data-Driven Approaches for Predicting the Natural Frequencies of Masonry Minarets
papers.abstract: Historical masonry minarets are particularly susceptible to earthquake-induced damage because their slender configuration is combined with the inherently low tensile capacity and limited ductility of masonry. Reliable characterization of their dynamic properties is therefore an important prerequisite for seismic evaluation and the planning of appropriate conservation measures. In this study, a data-driven methodology is developed to estimate the first and second natural frequencies of masonry minarets. A database comprising 1146 finite element models with different mechanical properties, representing 191 unique geometry groups, was developed through parametric modal analyses in Abaqus. The predictor set comprised total height H, lower and upper inner diameters D0 and Dtop, wall thickness t, base dimension B, and the stiffness–density-related parameter E/ρ. Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost models were evaluated using geometry-grouped nested five-fold cross-validation, while explicit equations were derived using linear and symbolic regression. CatBoost achieved the best overall machine-learning performance, with mean outer-test R2 values of 0.9597 and 0.9610 for f1 and f2, respectively. SHAP analyses identified total height and E/ρ as the dominant predictors. Symbolic regression provided substantially more accurate explicit equations than linear regression and achieved predictive performance comparable to the best machine-learning-based models. An additional mechanically scaled geometry-only baseline achieved mean outer-test R2 values of 0.8222 and 0.8217 for the first and second frequencies, respectively, improving on ordinary additive linear regression while remaining less accurate than the more flexible models. The proposed framework provides an accurate, interpretable, and computationally efficient surrogate for predicting finite element-derived natural frequencies within the investigated parameter domain. However, the reported predictive performance reflects agreement with the numerical reference models, and experimental validation is required before applying the proposed models to existing masonry minarets.

papers.title: Novel bicolumnar fixation with primary cup implantation for pelvic discontinuity in revision hip arthroplasty: a comparative clinical study
papers.abstract: Pelvic discontinuity is a rare but challenging condition in revision hip arthroplasty. Traditional cage-based reconstruction techniques often rely solely on mechanical fixation and may be associated with implant migration, loosening, and mechanical failure. Alternative strategies aimed at restoring pelvic continuity and achieving biological fixation may improve construct stability and clinical outcomes. This retrospective study included 19 patients with intraoperatively confirmed pelvic discontinuity who underwent revision total hip arthroplasty between 2014 and 2024. Patients were divided into three groups according to the reconstruction technique used: Group 1 ( n = 8) underwent anti-protrusio cage reconstruction alone, Group 2 ( n = 6) received additional anterior quadrilateral surface plating prior to cage implantation, and Group 3 ( n = 5) underwent restoration of pelvic continuity through anterior and posterior column fixation followed by implantation of a porous-coated primary acetabular cup. Clinical and radiological outcomes were assessed with a minimum follow-up of 2 years, including complications, loosening, reoperation, and reoperation-free survival. Nineteen patients (mean age 71.2 years) with intraoperatively confirmed pelvic discontinuity were included. Aseptic loosening rates differed significantly among the three groups ( P = 0.039), occurring in 50% of patients in Group 1 and in none of the patients in Groups 2 or 3. Reoperation rates were higher in Group 1 (75%) than in Group 2 (16.7%) and Group 3 (20%), although this difference did not reach statistical significance ( P = 0.074). Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated a trend toward lower reoperation-free survival in Group 1; however, differences among the groups were not statistically significant (log-rank P = 0.237). Reconstruction strategies involving restoration of pelvic continuity through column stabilization may provide improved mechanical stability and lower complication rates compared with conventional cage-only techniques in the management of pelvic discontinuity. In selected patients, bicolumnar fixation followed by implantation of a porous-coated primary acetabular cup may offer the additional advantage of biological fixation. Larger prospective studies are needed to validate these findings.

papers.title: AI-Enhanced finite element analysis for optimal material selection in total knee replacement
papers.abstract: The increasing prevalence of total knee replacement (TKR) surgery and its association with aseptic loosening present a significant research challenge. This issue can be mitigated by selecting optimal materials for TKR components. This paper presents a hybrid approach combining Finite Element Method (FEM) with Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques for optimal material selection in TKR. Simulations of four normal movements—compression, distraction, medial bending, and lateral bending—were performed on a 3D model of the artificial knee. Four materials were evaluated: Cobalt-Chromium (Co-Cr), Zirconium (Zr), Stainless Steel, and Titanium (Ti). To simulate ligamentous constraints during distraction loading, a model of a nonlinear spring element was included, furnishing more physiologically realistic boundary conditions. An Artificial Neural Network (ANN) was trained on FEM simulation data to predict material performance with 98.7% accuracy for stress prediction (R 2 = 0.987), while displacement prediction achieved R 2 = 0.985. Multi-criteria decision-making using TOPSIS ranked Co-Cr as the optimal material under stress-prioritized weighting (0.6/0.4); though, sensitivity analysis revealed that Stainless Steel converts optimal when displacement/compliance is prioritized (0.4/0.6). Under axial compression of 1300 N, maximum stress for Co-Cr and Zr was 4.207 × 10 8 N/m 2 and 3.921 × 10 8 N/m 2 , respectively. Under distraction: 4.321 × 10 8 N/m 2 and 4.142 × 10 8 N/m 2 . Under medial bending: 1.101 × 10 8 N/m 2 and 1.088 × 10 8 N/m 2 . Under lateral bending: 1.119 × 10 8 N/m 2 and 1.102 × 10 8 N/m 2 . The AI-based approach reduced computational time by 73% compared to full FEM simulations while maintaining high prediction accuracy. This time-saving shows the promise of the surrogate model for large scale materials screening and patient specific implant optimization, but further biocompatibility and tribological validation will be required for clinical translation of these findings.

papers.title: Embedding Consistent Recurrent Neural Networks for Fracture Modelling in Large Scale Shell Structures
papers.abstract: Data-driven surrogates could replace phenomenological fracture criteria in structural-scale shell element simulations, but a recurrent surrogate can operate inside an explicit solver only if its predictions are independent of the increment count. This condition was tested by embedding a trained recurrent neural network (RNN) localisation surrogate as the erosion criterion in an Abaqus finite element material subroutine. A SimpleRNN was compared against the proposed consistent RNN (ConsRNN), whose transition function makes predictions converge with increasing increment count. Both were trained on 19,098 bilinear strain paths from solid-element simulations of one structural steel. At the 400-increment training resolution, the SimpleRNN was more accurate but drifted with the increment count, whereas the embedded ConsRNN’s prediction varied by only 1.5% between 400 and 200,000 increments. In a clamped steel plate indented to rupture, the force–displacement curves coincided to the peak for network sampling intervals differing by over an order of magnitude. The ConsRNN and an experimentally validated two-factor-scaling (2FS) criterion for the same steel predicted nearly identical fracture onset and peak force at indistinguishable computational cost. No benefit from the surrogate’s history dependence was demonstrated, because the crack-path elements were loaded nearly proportionally, and ranking the criteria requires a fracture experiment. The paper’s main contribution is the embedding of a customised recurrent cell with a non-standard transition function as a live fracture criterion in a structural-scale explicit FE analysis.

papers.title: Acoustic analysis comparison and model optimization of Chinese ancient and modern oboes
papers.abstract: As a traditional Chinese double-reed woodwind instrument, the Suona has evolved through representative forms such as the Tang dynasty Bili and Qing dynasty Sunaiyi. However, systematic studies on its acoustic characteristics across historical evolution remain scarce. This work takes the Qing dynasty Sunaiyi and the modern standard Suona as samples, and adopts an integrated approach combining three-dimensional scanning, finite element simulation, and intelligent optimization. High-fidelity axisymmetric finite element models are built based on historical records and scanning data. The two instruments are compared in far-field sound pressure level, directivity, central-axis pressure distribution, and internal sound field, followed by parametric optimization of the modern Suona bell profile. Results show that the Sunaiyi has a longer tube and gentler bell flare and exhibits higher overtone frequencies and unstable high-order overtones. In contrast, the modern Suona, with a shorter tube and steeper bell flare, achieves a lower fundamental overtone, smoother far-field attenuation, and more concentrated directivity. Spectral measurements in a professional studio agree well with simulations, validating the numerical models. A surrogate-assisted K‑means clustering particle swarm optimization algorithm with diversity control (SAPSO‑BCM) is proposed and coupled with COMSOL for global optimization of bell curvature to obtain the optimal radian values under different sound pressure level targets. This work pioneers the integrated three‑dimensional scanning, FEM, and intelligent optimization workflow for Suona acoustics, investigating the influence of structural parameters on radiation performance and offering a generalizable engineering method for traditional wind instruments.

papers.title: The gut-bone axis: gut microbiota dysbiosis and dental implant failures – Is there a link? - A narrative review
papers.abstract: Introduction The gut microbiota plays a pivotal role in systemic health, particularly in bone metabolism and periodontal integrity, through the gut–bone axis. Emerging evidence suggests that gut microbiota dysbiosis may indirectly contribute to dental implant failure by disrupting bone homeostasis and aggravating periodontal disease. Despite growing recognition of this relationship, comprehensive understanding of the underlying mechanisms and therapeutic strategies remains limited. This review explores the available biological evidence on the impact of gut microbiota dysbiosis on dental implant failures. Methods A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and related databases was performed following PRISMA guidelines. Studies addressing the gut microbiota–bone health connection, gut microbiota–periodontium interactions, and their collective influence on implant success were included. Screening was based on predefined criteria, with data extraction focusing on mechanisms through which dysbiosis affects osseointegration and peri-implant health. Results The review revealed a strong association between gut dysbiosis and altered bone metabolism, impairing osseointegration and raising the risk of implant failure. Gut dysbiosis also exacerbated periodontal inflammation, predisposing to peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis. Non-invasive strategies such as probiotics, prebiotics, and targeted dietary modifications showed promise in restoring microbial balance, attenuating systemic inflammation, and supporting peri-implant tissue health. However, wide heterogeneity in study design and methodology restricted the strength and comparability of available evidence. Conclusion Gut microbiota dysbiosis is an emerging and underrecognized risk factor for implant failure. Modulating dysbiosis through non-invasive interventions may enhance osseointegration and peri-implant tissue integrity. Nevertheless, most current evidence arises from preclinical or small-scale human studies, highlighting the urgent need for robust, large-scale clinical trials.

papers.title: In-situ bioprinting at bioactive wound interfaces: A clinically driven design-rule framework
papers.abstract: Chronic and complex wounds exist within heterogeneous, unstable clinical environments characterized by irregular geometry, persistent exudate, bleeding, and strict time constraints at the bedside. Despite advances in biomaterials, skin substitutes, and bioprinting technologies, most wound-healing strategies are still developed and validated under controlled laboratory conditions that fail to capture these realities, contributing to limited clinical translation. In-situ bioprinting reframes wound treatment as an on-site biofabrication problem, enabling the direct deposition of bioactive constructs onto living tissue at the point-of-care. However, current literature remains largely material- and technology-centered, with no unified framework that links real wound constraints to printable design parameters. In this mini-review, we establish a clinically driven design-rule framework that systematically maps on-wound constraints to key printable parameters, including gelation kinetics, viscosity windows, spatial patterning, and degradation behavior. By synthesizing recent experimental and translational studies, we map these parameters to clinically relevant outcomes such as rapid hemostasis, infection control, angiogenesis, and long-term tissue remodeling. We further identify wound-edge heterogeneity as one important but underappreciated constraint among several interacting factors that shape design requirements and outline translational and regulatory challenges unique to point-of-care biofabrication. By shifting the focus from material composition to constraint-driven design logic, this work provides a practical framework for developing clinically robust in-situ bioprinting strategies.

papers.title: Primary Stability of an Expandable Versus a Conventional Short Implant in Low-Density Bone: A Density-Stratified Ex Vivo Comparison
papers.abstract: Background: Rehabilitation of atrophic posterior jaws is often challenging due to anatomical limitations, frequently requiring bone augmentation procedures or the use of short implants. Expandable short implants are characterized by an expansion mechanism whose potential contribution to primary stability remains to be fully established. This ex vivo study compared the primary stability of expandable and conventional short implants in porcine rib bone of low and intermediate CBCT-defined density (corresponding approximately to Misch D4 and D3). Methods: A total of 68 implants were placed in 17 fresh porcine ribs, using a randomized complete block design: 34 expandable short implants (ESI; Pyramidion, Ø4.1 × 5 mm) and 34 conventional short implants (CSI; Osstem TS III, Ø4 × 7 mm), equally distributed between two CBCT-defined density strata (D3 and D4, operationally defined). Peak insertion torque (PIT), resonance frequency analysis (ISQ; before and after apical expansion for the ESI group), peak removal torque (PRT), and expansion torque (ESI group only) were recorded. Data were analyzed using a two-way ANOVA (implant group × bone density) with a Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold (α = 0.025) for the two primary outcomes, ISQ and PRT. Results: PIT did not differ significantly between groups in D3 bone, while CSI showed higher PIT in D4 bone (p = 0.0005). ISQ increased significantly following apical expansion in the ESI group (mean + 4.91, 95% CI 3.60 to 6.22; p = 0.0004), more markedly in D4 than D3 bone; final ISQ did not differ significantly between groups at either bone density. PRT was higher in the ESI group in both density strata (p = 0.0004 in D3 and p = 0.0003 in D4), with no significant implant group × bone density interaction. Incomplete apical expansion occurred in 3 of 34 ESI implants, all in D3 bone. Conclusions: In this ex vivo model, no statistically significant difference in final ISQ was detected between the expandable and conventional short implants, and removal torque was higher for the expandable implant across both bone densities; equivalence was not tested. papers.title: Asymmetric deformation modelling and fast adaptive MPC for slab camber control in hot rough rolling
papers.abstract: Slab camber is a critical shape-defect problem in hot strip rough rolling and directly affects slab centring, side-guide interaction and subsequent rolling stability. Excessive slab camber is especially problematic during transient threading stages, particularly at the head end, where asymmetric rolling conditions are more pronounced. To address this problem, this article proposes a physics-guided analysis and fast control method based on asymmetric deformation modelling. A mathematical model of slab camber motion is established by considering the combined effects of incoming wedge, initial curvature, centre offset, and stiffness difference. Based on this model, the influences of different asymmetric factors on exit wedge evolution and transient lateral motion are quantitatively analysed in an interpretable manner. Accordingly, an auto-tuning method for fast model predictive control (F-MPC) with an adaptive time horizon is proposed to dynamically suppress slab camber. The optimal time-horizon combination is obtained by particle swarm optimisation (PSO) for offline optimisation, and the online computational burden is reduced by an interior-point method with warm-start initialisation to satisfy control-cycle requirements. Simulations and mill trials show that the F-MPC controller effectively reduces slab camber at the roughing-mill exit and is suitable for industrial online implementation.

papers.title: Compressive behavior and energy absorption of SLM-fabricated diamond-TPMS tube reinforced with bionic spider-web ribs
papers.abstract: Aluminum alloy thin-walled tubes are widely used in lightweight energy-absorbing structures owing to their high specific strength and crashworthiness. However, Diamond-type triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) tubes may exhibit unstable penetrating 45° shear band deformation under axial compression. To mitigate this instability, a bionic spider-web rib-reinforced Diamond-TPMS tube (D-BCT) is proposed based on spatial–structural partitioning, dividing the annular region into an inner rib-reinforced region and an outer Diamond-TPMS region. Three specimens of each structure were fabricated from AlSi10Mg alloy by selective laser melting and tested under quasi-static axial compression. Within a common 0–15 mm evaluation displacement, the D-BCT achieved a mean specific energy absorption (SEA) of 38.74 J/g, approximately 9.9% higher than that of the conventional Diamond-TPMS tube (D-CT), while reducing the mean peak crushing force by approximately 30.7% and increasing the mean crushing force efficiency (CFE) from 64.66% to 74.92%. Compared with D-CT, D-BCT exhibited progressive crushing and buckling rather than a penetrating shear band, together with a more stable plateau response. These results suggest that spatial–structural partitioning is a promising approach for improving the quasi-static crushing stability of Diamond-TPMS tubes.

papers.title: An Evaluation of Precision in Implant Placement During the Early Learning Curve for the Direct Anterior Approach in Total Hip Arthroplasty
papers.abstract: Background: Acquiring new skills is associated with a requisite learning curve, with potential for increased complications. While previous studies have evaluated complications associated with the learning curve for the direct anterior approach, no studies have evaluated whether there is a decrease in surgical precision during this formative period. The purpose of our study was to compare the precision of implant placement during a surgeon's early learning curve with the direct anterior (DA) approach for total hip arthroplasty (THA) with that of the surgeon's previous approach. Methods: Between 7/2012 and 3/2021, five surgeons converted from a posterior (PA) or anterolateral (AL) approach to a DA approach for primary THA. For each surgeon, initial cases using the DA approach were compared 1:1 with cases using the PA or AL approach before the transition. Radiographic parameters were recorded for each patient. Statistical analysis was conducted using the Bartlett test (precision) for homogeneity of variances and the F-test for pairwise comparisons of variances across surgical approaches. Results: A total of 618 patients were included. Across all surgeons, the DA approach was more precise with postoperative leg length ( P = 0.003) and femoral offset ( P = 0.009) when compared with the PA approach and more precise with leg length ( P = 0.016) when compared with the AL approach. No loss in precision was observed with the DA approach compared with the PA and AL approaches for acetabular inclination (all P < 0.05). Conclusion: The direct anterior approach demonstrated comparable or improved precision with implant positioning even during a surgeon's early learning curve.
